newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CSFB's Holbrooke won't rule out Swiss bank boycott.
newsitem.headline: CSFB's Holbrooke won't rule out Swiss bank boycott.

text.p: Credit Suisse First Boston Vice-chairman Richard Holbrooke said Swiss banks could still face a boycott from isolated critics who accuse the banks of hoarding the dormant wealth of Jews killed in the Holocaust.

Holbrooke, a former senior U.S. diplomat, ruled out the prospect that the U.S. government would join such a boycott, but he told reporters individuals could still launch a drive against the banks to push their own agenda.
"I, personally, do not think a boycott of that sort will happen or is a good idea," he said during a visit to Zurich.

"But I stress there are individuals who will take their own actions for whatever reasons, and it could hurt," he said. "I do not believe the U.S. government would participate in such a thing, but still, it could hurt."

Talk among Jewish groups of calling a boycott of Swiss banks swelled when Swiss Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz in December dismissed as "blackmail" Jewish calls for quick Swiss restitution for Holocaust victims.

The calls waned after Delamuraz, then finishing a one-year term as Swiss president, apologised for the comment, which came amid accusations Swiss banks were sitting on billions of dollars of wealth Jews stashed in Switzerland to escape the Nazi terror.
And Holbrooke played down the chances mainstream Jewish groups would now call a boycott, noting the efforts Switzerland has made to cast light on its wartime role as financial centre.
"I don't think it will come to that. Leaders on both sides are much too aware of the problem," he said.

Holbrooke said business at CSFB, the investment banking arm of Credit Suisse Group, had not yet suffered from the controversy, though many clients had raised the issue. "I think we have a loyal group of clients who know that Credit Suisse has been in the forefront of trying to solve this problem. I don't think it has done us any damage at all at this point."
